summary: When requesting a certificate, the subject normally proves it holds the private key. This document specifies an attribute that lets the subject state that it possesses the private key instead, for cases where a CA might accept such a statement.

eli5.summary: Usually you show your key to prove it is yours. Here you may simply say "I have the key" in a written note when the certificate office agrees that is enough.

subtitle: A signed statement that lets a certificate requester claim it holds a private key, instead of proving it.

tldr.problem: A CA normally demands proof that a requester holds the private key for the public key being certified, but some key types, such as ML-KEM keys, are awkward to prove possession for in PKCS#10 requests.
tldr.mechanism: The requester adds a privateKeyPossessionStatement attribute to its certificate request and signs the request with a signature key whose certificate was issued earlier to the same subject. The CA validates that signature and certificate path and accepts the claim if its policy allows.
tldr.outcome: A subject with separate signature and key establishment certificates can get the second one with a simple signed statement. The catch is that a lost signature key lets someone else make the statement.

today: RFC 9883 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2025. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
X.509 certificate enrollment often uses PKCS#10 or the Certificate Request Message Format (CRMF). A Certification Authority (CA) typically demands proof of possession of the private key matching the public key to be certified. This RFC defines an alternative: a signed statement from the subject claiming it holds that private key.

The motivating case is a subject needing separate certificates for signing and for key establishment, for example an ML-DSA signature key with an ML-KEM key establishment key, or ECDSA with ECDH. A statement validated with the earlier signature certificate may be enough to issue the second certificate, if the Certificate Policy allows it.

The RFC notes that RFC 6955 offers proof-of-possession algorithms for Diffie-Hellman keys, but they are not suitable for PKCS#10 and do not support key encapsulation algorithms such as ML-KEM. The new attribute works with both PKCS#10 and CRMF.
sections.eli5: Normally you prove a key is yours by using it. Sometimes that is hard, so this lets you sign a note saying you have it, and the certificate office can choose to trust the note.

sections.title: The Two-Certificate Flow
sections.content:
With PKCS#10 the subject first generates a signature key pair, sends a normal certificate signing request signed with that key, and receives a signature certificate with a key usage of digitalSignature, nonRepudiation or both.

Then it generates the key establishment key pair and sends a second request containing the new public key. This request carries the new attribute, uses the same subject name as before and is signed with the first private key. The CA returns a key establishment certificate with a key usage of keyEncipherment or keyAgreement.

Usually both certificates come from the same issuer. If the issuers differ, the second issuer's certificate policy MUST explain how it verifies the subject and subject alternative names.
sections.eli5: First you get an ID card by proving who you are. Later, to get a second card, you show up with a note signed using the first card, saying you have what is needed.

sections.title: The Possession Statement Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute says: the subject of the signature certificate that validates this request's signature states, without providing proof, that it possesses the private key matching the request's public key. Its value is a PrivateKeyPossessionStatement with a signer (the issuer and serial number of the signature certificate) and an optional cert (the signature certificate itself). The cert MAY be omitted when the same CA issued the signature certificate and can look up its own certificates. The attribute OID is 1.3.6.1.4.1.22112.2.1.

The CA MUST validate the certification path of the signature certificate and MUST validate the request's signature with its public key, rejecting the request if either fails. The subject, and any subject alternative names, SHOULD match those in the signature certificate. If they differ, certificate policy MUST say how to decide they are the same entity, and the CA MUST reject the request if it cannot. When rejecting, the CA should tell the requester why and should log the event.
sections.eli5: The note says who signed it and, optionally, includes a copy of their ID card. The certificate office checks that the ID is valid, that the signature matches and that the names agree before saying yes.

sections.title: Use in PKCS#10 and CRMF
sections.content:
In a PKCS#10 request, the subject name SHOULD match the signature certificate, subjectPKInfo MUST hold the key establishment public key, and the attributes MUST include the possession statement. The signature algorithm MUST be one that the signature certificate's public key can validate, and certification path validation MUST succeed.

For CRMF the same attribute is reused under the names regCtrl-privateKeyPossessionStatement and id-regCtrl-statementOfPossession. The certTemplate MUST include subject and publicKey. The proof of possession MUST use the signature CHOICE, with poposkInput present, the sender CHOICE for authInfo and a signature validating with the signature certificate. The regInfo attributes MUST include the statement.
sections.eli5: There are two request forms in use. In both, the note goes in the same place and the whole request is signed with the earlier signature key.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The attribute MUST NOT be used to obtain a signature certificate, since proving possession of a signature key is easily done by signing the request. The statement is not technical proof: if the subject loses control of the signature private key, another party could generate the signed statement. Timely revocation of the compromised signature certificate is the only protection, and the CA SHOULD then also revoke every key establishment certificate obtained using statements signed by it.

The signature key pair SHOULD be at least as strong as the key establishment key pair, so the statement is not the weakest link. If subject names or alternative names differ from the signature certificate, certificate policy MUST describe how to decide they identify the same entity.
sections.eli5: If someone steals your signing key, they can write the note pretending to be you. So if a key is stolen, the office must cancel its ID and the cards that were issued because of it.
